Mike Markkula

Mike Markkula is a prominent figure in the history of Apple Inc., best known for his role as the company's second CEO from 1981 to 1983. He was a crucial early investor, providing $250,000 in funding during Apple's formation in 1977, and is often credited with bringing essential business acumen and organizational skills to the company, helping to stabilize and guide its young founders, Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak. Born on February 11, 1942, in Los Angeles, California, Markkula earned degrees in electrical engineering from the University of Southern California and had a successful career in companies like Intel and Fairchild Semiconductor before joining Apple.

During his tenure, Apple became the first personal computer company to reach $1 billion in sales, and Markkula's insights into marketing and business strategy contributed significantly to this growth. He later served as chairman of Apple's board until 1997 and remained influential in various capacities even after stepping back from daily operations. In addition to his work at Apple, Markkula co-founded Echelon Corporation and has been involved in philanthropic efforts, particularly in the field of ethics in technology through his contributions to Santa Clara University. His legacy is recognized as pivotal to Apple's early successes, though he often worked behind the scenes.

What is SIDS?

Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) is the sudden and unexplained death of a baby younger than 1 year old. A diagnosis of SIDS is made if the baby's death remains unexplained even after a death scene investigation, an autopsy, and a review of the clinical history.

SIDS is part of a larger category of unexpected (as opposed to unexplained) infant deaths called SUDI (sudden unexpected death in infancy). Babies who die suddenly but whose causes of death are later explained (infection, brain abnormality, cardiac dysfunction, etc.) also fall into this SUDI category.

Who is at risk for SIDS?

SIDS is a mysterious syndrome, since by its very definition the cause cannot be determined. But certain risk factors do exist.

About 2,300 babies in the United States die of SIDS each year. Some babies are more at risk than others. For example, SIDS is more likely to affect a baby who is between 1 and 4 months old, it is more common in boys than girls, and most deaths occur during the fall, winter and early spring months.

By Patricia Hartley

When you are new to family history research, it's easy to imagine that every ancestor will fit neatly into a perfect family group: father, mother and children. They'll live together in one household in the census, share the same last name, and first births will occur at least nine months after a marriage.

It doesn't take long to discover, though, that our ancestors' lives were as complicated as ours are today. They divorced, lived together without marrying, cheated on their spouses, and had children before marriage (or even while they were married to someone else).

Sometimes you stumble upon these mysterious children or illogical dates by accident, and then work to figure out how this person came about. Other times, you suspect a child was born outside your expected typical family group and focus your research on proving their legitimacy or "illegitimacy."
